description:
Get Stencil Group Buy: Make Social Graphics From One Campaign Brief

Stencil is a browser-based graphic design tool for assembling images, text, and simple layouts. Its feature pages describe templates, image uploads, cropping, preset sizes, and resizing. These capabilities suit recurring work such as making a set of announcement graphics, creating blog artwork, or adapting an approved message to multiple placements. The SEOGBTools listing is a separate access offer. Confirm which controls and allowances come with that offer if your project depends on a particular export size, uploaded font, or saved template.

A useful first Stencil project is a campaign that needs the same message in three places. Imagine a neighborhood bookshop announcing a Saturday reading. The shop wants a square feed post, a vertical story, and a wide header for its event page. Each format must make the event recognizable. Each also gives you different amounts of room for a photograph, headline, and date.

Gather the copy and photo before opening a template

Write down the event name, date, time, address, and booking instructions. Ask who can approve those details. For the bookshop, the first customer question might be whether they need a ticket. If seats are free but require a reservation, use the same approved wording every time. A draft that says “Free entry” may invite people to turn up without booking if the reservation condition only appears in a caption.

Choose a photograph that supports the message. A photo of the reading area can help people recognize the space. A portrait of the author works if you have permission to use it. If the only available portrait is tightly cropped, try using it in a separate frame beside the text rather than spreading it across the entire background. Keep the original image so you can try another crop without enlarging an already reduced export.

Decide what each placement should do. The square post might tell people the event is happening. The story can prompt immediate registration. The event header helps a visitor confirm that they opened the right page. A square tile can carry a date and author name while the page heading carries the rest. This makes the artwork less crowded and keeps key details available as page text.

Choose a template by how it handles your real text

Open a design close to the intended placement. Replace the sample headline and date before adjusting decoration. Template text is often selected to fit a particular line length. A real author name or an unusually long event title may wrap differently. If wrapping pushes the date below the visible area, try another layout or make room by reducing background detail.

Read the hierarchy without looking at the source brief. The first thing you see should be the piece of information that tells you what the graphic is about. For a bookshop reading, that may be the author name or the event format. The next visible element should give the viewer a reason to keep reading. A clear date generally matters more than a decorative strip or a second logo.

Use one text style for the headline and a simpler style for details. Keep a consistent left edge if you stack several lines. A narrow column may be appropriate for a story, but a date written in large type over four lines can leave too little room for the photo. Test the layout with the actual longest value you will need. If the next event has a longer venue name, that name should fit without an emergency redesign.

Crop around the subject and the text area

Begin with the source photo and identify the part that must remain visible. In a portrait, check the person's face, gaze, and position. In a photograph of the venue, choose a detail that identifies the place. A picture with the subject near the edge may be useful if the opposite side provides clear space for text. A centered photo may work better as a separate picture block.

Use Stencil’s image crop controls to try the layout at the intended aspect ratio. Zooming in can remove clutter, but it also reduces the usable image area. Check where the crop falls around the top of a head, the edge of a book, or another detail that readers need to recognize. Then look at the same picture at its intended display size. A photo that looks crisp in the editor can show softness after a tight crop and export.

If the photo competes with the lettering, test moving the type into a solid color area. You can also use a simpler part of the original background. Compare both on a phone before choosing. Thin white text over a bookcase may be readable in one spot and disappear over a pale book spine a few letters later. Keep essential details on a background that offers steady contrast across the whole line.

Resize the design and recheck every placement

Once the square version is approved, make a copy for the story. If resizing is available in your workspace, use it to set the intended canvas, then inspect what moved. A wider photograph may crop to just a face in a vertical design. The logo may look unusually large compared with the new width. Put the headline and photo where they fit the story, then move secondary details to a separate panel if the layout becomes crowded.

Review the vertical version in a preview that shows where platform controls appear. Important copy too close to the top may compete with the account name. Text at the bottom may sit behind a reply or navigation control. The safest location depends on where the file will run. Check the actual placement on a device before declaring the export finished.

For the website header, open the page preview at desktop and mobile widths. Some templates crop an image to fill the header area, so the edges you see in the design editor may be absent online. If the headline is already written as page text, the header can use a closer photograph and leave the words to the page. This gives you more freedom to crop without making the event details disappear.

Prepare useful variants for recurring events

A reusable layout should allow future editors to change the information that regularly changes. For a monthly bookshop event, that includes the author name, portrait, date, and signup instructions. The store colors and logo can stay in predictable positions. Test the layout with two sample events before deciding it works as a template. A second date and a longer name can reveal problems that the first graphic concealed.

Keep the design organized around the date and the placement. One naming pattern is event name, placement, and revision. A filename such as saturday-reading-story-v2.png tells a colleague which asset to upload. The source file or saved design can use the same stem. Put older exports in a separate folder after approval to reduce the chance that someone publishes a graphic with a previous time.

Make a short note about which fonts, images, and marks belong to the campaign. Include the person who can approve substitutions. A new designer may need to use a second font if the uploaded one is unavailable in their workspace. Decide which style characteristics matter, such as a wide headline or a readable numeral, so replacement choices support the established layout.

Check image rights and readable exports

Keep a record of where the original photograph came from. For an author portrait, check that the supplied permission covers the ways you plan to distribute the graphic. Consider the difference between a post for the store's followers, a public event page, and a paid ad. If a different approval is needed for an ad, resolve it before handing the design to the advertiser.

Choose the file type according to the destination. If the workspace offers more than one export format, compare a small photograph-heavy asset with a type-heavy graphic. Fine lettering can show compression around its edges. A website may optimize uploaded files again, so open the rendered page after upload. Check the letter edges, the image crop, and the darkest parts of the photograph under normal phone brightness.

Store the approved copy separately. If the start time changes, the person updating the graphic should have the correct time before opening a design. Review other places where the old time might appear, such as the event page heading, scheduled posts, and an email banner. When the images and corresponding copy are maintained together, changes can be applied without relying on someone remembering every version.

Run a review that catches errors before posting

Give the reviewer the three exports and a short note showing where each one will go. Ask them to identify the event, date, and booking action without reading the design brief. If they can read the headline but miss the date, change the visual hierarchy or move the date to a clearer part of the layout. If they cannot tell whether they need to book, clarify the words before spending time on decoration.

Verify ordinary details as carefully as the art. Compare the spelling of the guest's name with the event page. Check the numeric date against the named day of the week. Open the booking link from the actual post or story preview. Those checks help prevent a professional-looking design from sending people to the wrong page.

For the event page, add alt text that reflects why the image is present. A photo of a person can identify the author when that information helps the reader. If the image simply repeats a nearby heading and has no additional meaning, consider whether the destination allows empty alt text. Keep necessary facts in visible page text so people can still understand the event when the artwork is unavailable.

Decide whether the plan supports your workflow

Ask which Stencil workspace you will be using and how access begins. If you need to keep editable files, confirm whether your creations can remain available for future revisions. If your brand requires a particular typeface, confirm whether your access supports uploading it and whether you have permission to use it. If your work depends on a minimum download size, request the exact export options and test a sample.

A group-buy offer may be attractive for occasional work. A recurring studio workflow can depend on longer access and reliable ownership of its materials. Compare the cost with the time needed to rebuild a graphic if files cannot be carried over. Keep the original photos, approved wording, and final exports with your team so one missing workspace does not stop the next announcement.

Before choosing a subscription duration, try a real three-format project. Time the parts that matter. Record how long it took to build one version, adapt the next two, check the proofs, and correct an approved detail. A template is valuable when it shortens revisions as well as initial design. If the output works but resizing introduces several manual fixes, reflect that time in the decision.

Frequently asked questions

Can I upload my own product or event photos?

Stencil describes image uploads on its official feature page. Confirm that uploads are available in the workspace included with your offer and test a sample before using a deadline-sensitive campaign. Keep the original file outside the editor so you can reuse it for a different crop.

Will one design work for every social placement?

Start from the same message and photograph, then review each canvas separately. A story may need a taller crop, and a feed post may need larger text to stay readable at thumbnail size. A quick device check helps you avoid putting important information behind platform controls.

How do I keep graphics consistent across a series?

Pick a small group of colors and use repeatable positions for recurring information. Try the layout with both short and long headings before using it as a template. Save an approved reference along with the original photography and copy so another editor can reproduce the look.

What should I confirm before ordering?

Confirm the workspace, access period, export options, and any limits that affect the work you plan to do. Ask about saved designs or font uploads when those features matter to you. Test one graphic at the actual size you need and open it where readers will see it.

Your first campaign can be small. Make one event announcement, adapt it to your other placements, and check the exports in context. Keep the best layout and record how it handles a new headline or image. The next design then begins with a tested structure and accurate information.
